transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I'm here because... honestly, everyone keeps acting like I'm just imagining it, like my mind is playing tricks on me or something. But I know what I see. I've been a housekeeper for a long time, so I know my routine, I know my routes. I do the residential places out by the highway on Tuesdays, and the downtown offices on Thursdays, and I always take the exact same roads. But lately, I just know the hospital people—and I'm pretty sure some folks from the agency, too—have been watching our house. 

And not just the house, they're actually following me on my cleaning routes. I'll be taking the trash out at one of my client's homes, or shaking out a rug, and I'll see them parked right there down the street. They're doing it to see if I'm taking proper care of my husband. Which is just ridiculous, because I do absolutely everything for him. I make sure he's fed, his clothes are clean, his medications are sorted—I mean, I clean for a living, so you can imagine our house is spotless. But they just don't trust me, I guess. They want to catch me slipping up with his care. 

And it's just so frustrating when I try to tell people about these cars and these agency people keeping tabs on me, and they just brush it off and look at me like I'm making it up. But they are there. I see them when I leave for work at six in the morning, just sitting there watching the driveway, and they follow me all the way to my first house. I just wish they would knock on the door and ask me how he's doing instead of sneaking around while I'm trying to work.
Do you think these people are trying to harm you or your husband in any way?

Harm us? Oh, no, no, I don't think that. Lord, no. I mean, I haven't seen any weapons or anyone trying to break in or anything scary like that, thank goodness. If they really wanted to hurt us, they could have done it a long time ago, especially with my husband being home all day by himself in his recliner while I'm out scrubbing floors and dusting baseboards over at the highway properties. So, no, it’s not a violent thing at all. 

It's... well, it's more like an evaluation, you know? A secret, ongoing evaluation. They just want to find a reason to say I'm not fit to look after him. They want to catch me slipping up, maybe leaving him alone too long, or not getting his prescriptions filled on time—which I always do, by the way. I go to that little pharmacy over on Main Street every single month on the third, regular as clockwork, right after my morning shift. I never miss a refill. I even have one of those plastic pill organizers with the days of the week on it for him. But they don't know that, or they don't believe it. 

So they just sit out there in those cars, sipping their coffees, probably taking notes on their phones about how long it takes me to bring the garbage bins back up the driveway or what time I leave the house. So no, not harm. Just... snooping. Meddling in our business. Trying to build some kind of case against me, I suppose. It's just so exhausting, having to look over my shoulder constantly when all I'm trying to do is make an honest living and keep my own house in order.
Have you ever thought that there might be another explanation for the cars you see, or do you believe it's definitely the hospital people and the agency following you?

Another explanation? Well, I mean, I've tried to think of one. I really have. My sister-in-law, Brenda, she tells me, "Oh, it's just commuters, it's just people taking a shortcut because of the construction on Route 9." And sure, there is construction over there, they've been fixing those potholes since April, but these cars aren't taking a shortcut. Commuters don't just sit idling at the end of a cul-de-sac at 6:15 in the morning while I'm loading my mop bucket and my Clorox into the trunk. 

I know people keep acting like I'm just imagining it, like my mind is playing tricks on me because I work long hours or something, but I know what I see. I'm not stupid. I know for an absolute fact it is the hospital people, and definitely some folks from the agency, too. I've seen them looking right at me. They are watching our house, and they are following me on my cleaning routes, plain as day. 

Like I was saying before, they are doing it to see if I'm taking proper care of my husband. And it makes no sense to me, because if they just looked at the man, he's perfectly fine! He's eating three square meals a day—I made him a beautiful meatloaf just last night with the mashed potatoes he likes, the red-skinned ones, not the boxed kind. I don't ever use the boxed kind, I boil them and mash them myself with a little bit of garlic salt. But they don't care about the meatloaf or the potatoes. They just want to catch me doing something wrong. So no, I don't think it's just random cars or commuters. I can't accept that it's anything else, because I've seen them with my own two eyes, following me from house to house. I just wish everyone would stop acting like I'm making up fairy tales when the proof is sitting right there at the end of my driveway.
Have you ever had any doubts that it's really the hospital people and the agency following you?

Doubts? No. No, I don't have any doubts, because... well, like I said, I know what I see. I'm the one out there every day, loading my supplies into the car, driving from house to house. I know people keep acting like I'm imagining it, my sister-in-law, my neighbors, even some of my clients look at me funny if I mention it. They just brush it off. But I am not imagining it. 

I know, I know in my bones, that the hospital people and some folks from the agency have been watching our house. And they watch my cleaning routes, too. They just want to see if I'm taking proper care of my husband. Which, again, I am! I do his laundry on Wednesdays, I make sure his pills are sorted out on Sundays so he's ready for the week, I cook all his meals from scratch. I just don't understand why they can't just come to the door and ask, "Hey, how is he doing?" instead of sneaking around behind my back, trailing me to the highway properties and the downtown offices. So, no, I don't doubt it for a second. I just wish everyone else would stop acting like I'm crazy for seeing what is right there in front of my face.
Have you ever considered that your beliefs about being followed might be wrong?

Wrong? No, no, I haven't considered that. How could I be wrong when I'm the one living it? I mean, I'm the one out there every single day. I'm the one who sees the same silver sedan parked by the Miller's house on Tuesday, and then suddenly, there it is again on Thursday when I'm over at the Smith's place three towns over. That's not a coincidence. You don't just accidentally follow a housekeeper across county lines. 

And I know... I know I'm here, talking to you, because people keep acting like I'm imagining it. My sister-in-law, like I said, and even my husband sometimes gives me this look, this tired look, when I tell him to keep the blinds drawn. They all think I'm just stressed from the work, from being on my feet all day, smelling bleach and ammonia until my head spins. But I know what I know. I know the hospital people and some folks from the agency have been watching our house. They watch my cleaning routes. They are doing it to see if I'm taking proper care of my husband. 

It's just so frustrating, Doctor. It really is. To have everyone look at you like you're the one who's lost the plot, when you're the only one paying attention. I'm not wrong about this. I'm just not. I just want them to leave me alone so I can do my job and take care of my home in peace, without feeling like I'm under a microscope every time I take the recycling out.
Have you ever considered the possibility, even if it's a small one, that there could be another explanation for what you're seeing?

Another explanation? Like what? Like it's just a coincidence that the same exact cars are idling at the end of my street at the crack of dawn and then showing up outside the office buildings I clean in the evenings? No. No, I haven't considered it, because it's just not possible. I mean, I try to be a reasonable person, I really do. I pay my taxes, I go to church on Easter and Christmas, I keep a clean house—spotless, actually, because that's my profession. You don't get to be a housekeeper for thirty years without knowing how to pay attention to details. I notice things. I notice when a rug has been shifted two inches to the left, I notice when someone has been using the guest bathroom towels, and I notice when people are following me. 

I know I keep repeating myself, and I know I'm sitting here in this chair because people keep acting like I'm imagining the whole thing. My sister-in-law Brenda, my husband, the neighbors... they all think I'm just making a mountain out of a molehill. But I'm not. I know for a fact, I know it in my heart and in my head, that the hospital people and some folks from the agency have been watching our house. They've been watching my cleaning routes. They just want to see if I'm taking proper care of my husband. And I don't know why they can't just see that I am! I mean, I do everything for that man. I iron his shirts, I make sure he has his favorite coffee—the French roast, not the cheap stuff in the plastic tub—and I make sure his blood pressure cuff is right there on the nightstand where he can reach it. I am doing my job as a wife. So why won't they just leave me alone? Why do they have to keep sneaking around in those cars? There isn't another explanation, Doctor. There just isn't.
Have you ever had a moment where you questioned your own belief about being followed?

Questioned it? Like, stopped and thought, "Oh, maybe I'm just making this all up?" No. Never. Not even for a split second. Because how could I? I mean, I know why you're asking. I know I'm sitting here in this clinic, talking to you, because people keep acting like I'm imagining it. My sister-in-law Brenda, she actually had the nerve to tell me I needed to get my eyes checked. Can you believe that? My eyes are fine! I can spot a cobweb in the corner of a ten-foot ceiling without my glasses, so I think I can spot a grown man sitting in a parked car across the street from my house. 

And my husband, bless his heart, he just sighs and turns the TV up louder when I tell him to stay away from the front windows. It breaks my heart, it really does, because I'm trying to protect him. I'm trying to keep our lives together. But I know what's happening. I know the hospital people and some folks from the agency have been watching our house. And they don't just stop at the house, they follow my cleaning routes, too! From the big colonial on Elm Street all the way to the little ranch houses out by the county line. They are doing all of this, spending all this time and gas money, just to see if I'm taking proper care of my husband. 

Which is just... it's insulting! It's deeply insulting to me as a wife and as a woman who has kept a meticulous home for over thirty years. I mean, what do they think they're going to find? That I'm leaving him to starve? I made him a pot roast just last night! With the little pearl onions and the carrots cut on a bias, exactly how he likes them. I fluffed his pillows, I gave him his evening pills right at 8:00 PM with a glass of room-temperature water. I am doing everything right! So why would I question what I'm seeing when it's happening right to me? I don't need to question it. I just need them to stop. I need them to realize I'm doing a good job and go bother somebody else.
Do you think it's possible that your husband might not notice these people following you, even if you're certain they are?

Well, of course he doesn't notice. My husband... he's a good man, he really is, but he's just not paying attention the way I am. He's sitting in his recliner, watching his shows, trying to rest. He doesn't see what's happening outside the window. And I guess that's why I'm the one sitting here in this office, right? I'm here because people keep acting like I'm imagining it, like I'm making it all up in my head. My husband, Brenda, all of them—they just don't see it. 

But just because he doesn't notice the cars doesn't mean they aren't there. I mean, I'm the one who's up at dawn, packing my cleaning supplies, driving from neighborhood to neighborhood. I see the same faces. I see the same vehicles. I know the hospital people and some folks from the agency have been watching our house. And they don't just stay at the house, they've been watching my cleaning routes, too. They follow me from the moment I leave the driveway until I get back home. 

And I know exactly why they're doing it. They're doing it to see if I'm taking proper care of my husband. They think I'm neglecting him or something, which is just ridiculous. I mean, I make sure his meals are hot, I keep his clothes pressed, I make sure the house is spotless. I do everything! But he doesn't see them watching us because he's inside, safe, while I'm out there dealing with it. So no, it doesn't surprise me that he doesn't notice. But that doesn't change the fact that they're out there. I know what I see, Doctor. I really do.
Do you think there's anything that could ever convince you that the hospital people and the agency are not following you?

Convince me? Well... no. Honestly, no. Because what would it take? Someone from the agency coming right up to my front door, ringing the bell, and saying, "Oh, don't mind us, we aren't following you"? People lie, Doctor. People lie all the time, especially when they're trying to catch you doing something wrong. 

Look, I know I sound like a broken record. I know exactly why we're going in circles here. I'm here because people keep acting like I'm imagining it. Every time I try to explain it to anyone, they look at me like I've lost my marbles. But I haven't! I am a very grounded person. I deal with dirt, and grime, and reality all day long. So I know what's going on. I know the hospital people and some folks from the agency have been watching our house. I see them. And it's not just the house—they've been watching my cleaning routes, too. Just yesterday, I was over at the Miller place—it’s a big split-level, lots of baseboards, takes me a solid three hours just to dust and mop the downstairs—and sure enough, there was that same dark blue sedan parked by the fire hydrant. You just can't tell me that's a coincidence. 

And I know exactly what it boils down to. They want to see if I'm taking proper care of my husband. Which is just... it drives me up the wall, because I am! I don't know how many times or how many ways I have to prove it. His sheets are washed twice a week in hot water, his diet is strictly low-sodium—I don't even buy canned soup anymore, I make it all from scratch—and I even track his water intake on a little yellow notepad right there on the refrigerator door. I am a devoted wife. I have kept my vows, in sickness and in health. 

So, no. Unless I suddenly go blind, nothing is going to convince me they aren't out there. I trust my own two eyes. I just wish everyone else would trust them, too, instead of making me sit here defending myself when I haven't done a single thing wrong.
Have you experienced any major life changes or stressful events recently that might be affecting your thoughts or feelings?

Stressful? Well, my goodness, I should say so. If you want to talk about stress, you just have to look at what happened with my husband. It was... let me think, it’s been about 1 year and 2 months now. He had this terrible heart issue, a major cardiac hospitalization, and I tell you, it nearly aged me ten years in a single week. I was practically living in that hospital waiting room, sitting in those stiff plastic chairs, drinking that awful powdered coffee from the machine down the hall, just praying and praying he was going to pull through. 

And he did, thank the good Lord, but when they finally let him come home, they handed me a stack of discharge instructions as thick as a telephone book. I had to completely overhaul our entire lives. The low-sodium diet I told you about, the strict medication schedule, making sure he doesn't exert himself—all while I'm still working my full cleaning routes every single day to keep a roof over our heads! 

So, honestly, Doctor, this whole change... all of this business with the cars and the people watching me, it's been going on for exactly that long, about 1 year and 2 months, right since after my husband's cardiac hospitalization. Because that's when they started paying attention to us. The hospital people, they know he was in there, they know exactly how sick he was, and they decided they needed to monitor me to make sure I'm following all their little rules. Which I am! I am doing it perfectly. But it is a tremendous amount of pressure to have that hanging over your head, day in and day out, for over a year. Always looking over your shoulder while you're just trying to carry the groceries in. So, yes, I'd say I've been under a lot of stress. Anyone would be in my shoes.
Do you think there's anything that could change your mind about the hospital people and the agency following you?

Doctor, I feel like we're just going around in circles now. Didn't we just cover this? Like I was saying just a few minutes ago, no. Absolutely not. Because why would I change my mind about something that is actually happening right in front of my face? 

I know exactly why I'm sitting in this chair talking to you right now—I'm here because people keep acting like I'm imagining it, like I'm just some tired old woman making up stories in her head to get attention. But I am not. I know the hospital people and some folks from the agency have been watching our house. I know it in my bones. And they don't just stop at the house, they've been watching my cleaning routes, too, all just to see if I'm taking proper care of my husband. 

Why on earth would I change my mind when the proof is sitting right there? Just Tuesday I was lugging my heavy Hoover vacuum up three flights of stairs at the Henderson place—which is absolute murder on my knees, by the way, but they insist on those thick shag carpets in the bedrooms—and there was that same car, just idling at the corner. I see the way they try to look away when I pull back the curtains. I see them writing things down. I just... I don't understand why I have to keep defending myself to everyone. I wash his clothes, I cook his meals, I keep him alive. I am doing everything the doctors told me to do. 

So no, my mind is made up because my eyes work perfectly fine. You could bring the mayor in here to tell me otherwise and I still wouldn't believe it, because I know what I live with every single day. Nothing is going to change my mind, Doctor. Nothing.
Do you think it's possible for you to consider alternative explanations for what you're experiencing, even if you don't believe they're true?

Alternative explanations? You mean... like pretending maybe I'm just seeing things? Or that I'm just stressed and confused? Doctor, I really don't mean to be difficult, I truly don't, but we just keep hammering at this same nail and it's already flush with the wood. 

I know exactly why I'm sitting in this office. I'm here because people keep acting like I'm imagining it! Everyone wants to find some... some psychological reason for what's happening, but there isn't one. Why on earth would I sit around and try to brainstorm alternative explanations when I already have the facts? I know the hospital people and those folks from the agency have been watching our house. I know they've been tailing me on my cleaning routes. I've told you this already, they are doing it to see if I'm taking proper care of my husband! It's not a mystery that needs solving, so there's no need for me to sit here and make up other reasons for it.

Just this morning, before I came in here, I was over at the Thompson place. I was on my hands and knees scrubbing the grout in their master bathroom—using a little bristled toothbrush, mind you, because that is absolutely the only way to get the soap scum out of those tiny little corners by the shower door—and I could just feel the eyes on me. I peeked out through the bathroom blinds, and sure enough, there was a man in a tan windbreaker just standing across the street, pretending to check his phone. 

So, no. I can't just "consider" that maybe it's a coincidence or maybe I'm just a tired old maid making things up. It is exhausting enough trying to keep my husband's blood pressure down, making sure his pills are sorted in that little plastic day-by-day organizer, and working my fingers to the bone at these houses every single day, without having to play make-believe for you and pretend that these people aren't breathing down my neck. The truth is the truth, Doctor, whether anyone wants to believe me or not.
Have you ever seen or heard anything that you knew wasn't really there?

Seen or heard things that weren't... well, now, that's a tricky way to put it, isn't it? "Wasn't really there." Because, Doctor, I hear it. I hear it as plainly as I'm hearing your voice right now in this little office with the humming fluorescent lights. 

It happens mostly when I'm at home, after I've finished up my last house for the day. I'll be in the kitchen, maybe wiping down the counters—I always use a vinegar and water mix, it's so much better for the granite than those harsh chemical sprays, and it doesn't leave streaks—and the house will be completely quiet. My husband will be resting in his recliner in the living room with the television off, because the noise bothers him since his hospital stay. It'll be dead silent. 

And then, right near the kitchen window, right by the sink where I keep the dish rack, I will hear a woman's voice. Just... speaking to me. It's not a whisper, it's not a mumble, it's clear as a bell, as if she is standing right there on the linoleum next to me. She tells me things I need to do. She'll say, "Check the deadbolts on the front door," or she'll tell me to go move his pills, to make sure they're out of sight from the window so the agency people can't see what medications he's taking. 

It startles me every single time, I won't lie to you. I'll drop my sponge and spin around, and there's nobody there. Just the refrigerator humming. But I know what I heard! I'm not deaf, my hearing is perfectly fine—I can hear a vacuum belt slipping from three rooms away. So when you ask if I hear things that "aren't there," I don't know how to answer that, because the voice is there. I hear her. She's trying to help me keep him safe, I think. Reminding me of all the things I have to keep track of, because Lord knows I have a million things on my plate with the low-sodium cooking and the cleaning and the people watching us. So yes, I hear her, right by the window. Clear as day.
Have you ever seen anything that you knew wasn't really there, like shadows or figures, when you were alone?

Doctor, I feel like I'm talking to a brick wall sometimes. I really do. Didn't I just finish telling you about this not two minutes ago? You're asking me about shadows and figures now, but I don't see ghosts or boogeymen sneaking around my living room. I don't have the time or the energy to be looking for shadows in the dark, not with all the deep cleaning I have to do for my clients and making sure my husband is comfortable and his blood pressure isn't spiking. 

But what I *do* experience, like I literally just explained to you, is the voice. Even when the house is completely quiet—and I mean pin-drop quiet, because the television is off and he's resting in his chair—I hear that woman's voice right near the kitchen window. I don't see a shadow standing there, I just hear her. And she is telling me to check the locks on the doors, or she's telling me to move his pills so the agency people can't snoop on what he's taking. 

It is so clear, Doctor. It's exactly as if she is standing right there on the linoleum next to me while I'm doing the dishes. I'll be standing there with my hands in the warm soapy water, scrubbing out a Tupperware container—because if you put the ones with tomato sauce in the dishwasher, they stain orange permanently, and I absolutely refuse to have stained Tupperware in my cabinets—and her voice will just cut right through the silence. So no, I'm not seeing figures or shadows. But I hear her, clear as a bell, telling me to lock up and hide the medicine. I really don't know how many different ways I can explain the exact same thing to you.
Do you see the woman who speaks to you near the kitchen window?

Doctor, are you... are you actually listening to the words coming out of my mouth? Or are you just reading off a list of questions on that clipboard? Because I swear we are going around in circles like a washing machine on the spin cycle. 

No. I do not see her. If I saw a strange woman standing in my kitchen, I would be dialing 911, not standing there scrubbing dishes! Like I just said, I will spin around when she speaks, and I'll drip soapy water all over the floor—which is just fantastic, because then I have to stop what I'm doing and wipe it up immediately before it seeps into the seams of the linoleum and ruins the adhesive—and there is absolutely no one there to look at. The kitchen is empty.

But the fact that I don't see her doesn't change the fact that even when the house is completely, utterly quiet, I hear her voice. Right near the kitchen window. She tells me to check the locks, she tells me to move his pills so the agency people can't find them... it is as clear as if she is standing right there next to the dish rack. I don't see a face, I don't see a body, I don't see a shadow. I just hear her. I really, truly do not know how I can make this any clearer for you.
Do you ever hear the woman's voice when you are not at home?

Well, no, not really when I'm out and about. See, when I'm at work, I've got the vacuum running, or the radio on—Mrs. Henderson likes to keep the classical station playing softly while I dust her sitting room, she says it keeps the energy in the house calm, which I suppose is fine, though it does put me to sleep if I'm trying to scrub baseboards—so there's always noise. And I'm focused. I have a routine. I do the dry dusting first, then the damp wiping, then the floors. You have to work top to bottom, otherwise you're just knocking dust onto things you've already cleaned, which is a rookie mistake. 

So no, I don't hear her then. It's really just... it's just when I'm home. And it's exactly like I've been telling you. It happens when the house is completely quiet. My husband is resting, the TV is off, no radio, no vacuum, just silence. And then, right there near the kitchen window, I hear her. The woman's voice. It's as clear as if she's standing right there on the linoleum next to me while I'm at the sink. And she's telling me to go check the deadbolts, or to make sure his pills are moved out of sight so the agency people can't see them. It's only ever right there in my own kitchen, in the quiet. I don't know why she only speaks to me there, but that's where she is.
Do you think the woman's voice near the kitchen window could be related to the people you believe are following you?

Well, of course it is! I mean... it has to be, doesn't it? Why else would she specifically tell me to hide his medication from the agency people? That’s the whole reason I’m even sitting here in this chair talking to you today, because my family and... well, everybody, really... they keep acting like I’m just imagining the whole thing. They look at me with this pitying little smile, like I'm just an exhausted old woman making things up out of thin air. 

But I am not stupid, Doctor. I know what I see. I know for an absolute fact that the hospital people and some folks from the agency have been watching our house. And not just the house, they follow my cleaning routes, too. I'll be driving from Mrs. Henderson's place over to my next client in the Oakwood subdivision—which, by the way, is a complete nightmare right now because they've been doing road work on Elm for three months and the dust gets all over my freshly washed car, it's just a mess—and I will see them. I see them keeping tabs on me. 

They are doing it because they want to see if I'm taking proper care of my husband. As if I haven't been doing everything for him! I make sure he's comfortable, I cook him his low-sodium meals so his blood pressure stays down, I keep a spotless, completely sanitary home for him to rest in. I am doing everything right. But they are looking for any little excuse to say I'm not doing a good enough job, so they watch me. They watch the house. So yes, when that voice in the kitchen tells me to move his pills so the agency people can't snoop, she knows exactly what they are up to. She's warning me about them, because she knows they're out there watching, even if everyone else in my life wants to pretend I'm just imagining it.
Do you ever see things that aren't really there when you're hearing the woman's voice?

Doctor, I... I feel like I'm talking to a brick wall here. I really do. Did you not hear what I just said a few minutes ago? I swear, I am trying my absolute hardest to be cooperative and answer all these questions, but you keep asking me the same things over and over, just slightly reworded. 

No, I do not see things that aren't there! I told you, I don't see a face, I don't see a shadow, I don't see a body. When I am standing at that kitchen sink—and I use a very specific sponge for the dishes, mind you, not the one I use for wiping down the counters, because cross-contamination is how people get sick, especially with my husband's immune system being what it is—I am just looking at the dishes, or out the window at the yard. The yard needs mowing, actually, the grass is getting entirely too high, but I just haven't had the time between work and taking care of him. 

But no, I don't see anything out of the ordinary. It is strictly the voice. Even when the house is completely, pin-drop quiet, I hear her voice right near the kitchen window. She tells me to check the locks, or she tells me to move his pills so the agency people can't find them. It is as clear as if she is standing right there on the linoleum next to me. But I don't *see* her. I don't see anything at all that isn't supposed to be there. Just the voice. I don't know how many different ways I can explain this to you, Doctor. I really don't.
Do you think it's possible that the people you believe are following you are just in the same places as you by coincidence?

Coincidence? Doctor, please. Coincidence is when you run into the mailman at the grocery store. Coincidence is not the same silver sedan parked three houses down when I pull out of my driveway, and then that very same sedan turning onto Elm Street right behind me when I'm on my way to Mrs. Henderson's. You know, I actually memorized the first three letters of the license plate—J-K-L—because I thought, well, maybe I am just tired. Maybe my mind is playing tricks on me because I've been up since 4:30 AM making sure my husband's breakfast is prepared exactly the way he needs it. He has to have his oatmeal made with water, not milk, and a very specific ratio of cinnamon, otherwise his stomach gets upset, and I simply cannot have him getting sick on top of everything else. 

But no, it's not a coincidence. I am sitting here in this office today specifically because everyone—my family, the neighbors, everyone—keeps acting like I am just imagining this whole thing. They think I'm just a paranoid old woman who spends too much time cleaning. But I know what I see. I know for a fact that the hospital people and the folks from the agency have been watching our house. And they watch my cleaning routes, too! I see them at the Oakwood subdivision, I see them near the grocery store when I stop to get his low-sodium broth. 

They are doing it because they want to catch me slipping up. They want to see if I'm taking proper care of my husband, and they are just waiting for me to make one little mistake so they can step in. As if I haven't dedicated every waking moment to keeping that house perfectly sanitized and keeping him comfortable! So no, Doctor, it is absolutely not a coincidence. They are out there, they are watching, and I am not crazy for seeing them, no matter what anyone else tries to tell you.

doctor.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

target_item.name: Delusions

patient.answer:
Well, I'm here because... honestly, everyone keeps acting like I'm just imagining it, like my mind is playing tricks on me or something. But I know what I see. I've been a housekeeper for a long time, so I know my routine, I know my routes. I do the residential places out by the highway on Tuesdays, and the downtown offices on Thursdays, and I always take the exact same roads. But lately, I just know the hospital people—and I'm pretty sure some folks from the agency, too—have been watching our house. 

And not just the house, they're actually following me on my cleaning routes. I'll be taking the trash out at one of my client's homes, or shaking out a rug, and I'll see them parked right there down the street. They're doing it to see if I'm taking proper care of my husband. Which is just ridiculous, because I do absolutely everything for him. I make sure he's fed, his clothes are clean, his medications are sorted—I mean, I clean for a living, so you can imagine our house is spotless. But they just don't trust me, I guess. They want to catch me slipping up with his care. 

And it's just so frustrating when I try to tell people about these cars and these agency people keeping tabs on me, and they just brush it off and look at me like I'm making it up. But they are there. I see them when I leave for work at six in the morning, just sitting there watching the driveway, and they follow me all the way to my first house. I just wish they would knock on the door and ask me how he's doing instead of sneaking around while I'm trying to work.

Harm us? Oh, no, no, I don't think that. Lord, no. I mean, I haven't seen any weapons or anyone trying to break in or anything scary like that, thank goodness. If they really wanted to hurt us, they could have done it a long time ago, especially with my husband being home all day by himself in his recliner while I'm out scrubbing floors and dusting baseboards over at the highway properties. So, no, it’s not a violent thing at all. 

It's... well, it's more like an evaluation, you know? A secret, ongoing evaluation. They just want to find a reason to say I'm not fit to look after him. They want to catch me slipping up, maybe leaving him alone too long, or not getting his prescriptions filled on time—which I always do, by the way. I go to that little pharmacy over on Main Street every single month on the third, regular as clockwork, right after my morning shift. I never miss a refill. I even have one of those plastic pill organizers with the days of the week on it for him. But they don't know that, or they don't believe it. 

So they just sit out there in those cars, sipping their coffees, probably taking notes on their phones about how long it takes me to bring the garbage bins back up the driveway or what time I leave the house. So no, not harm. Just... snooping. Meddling in our business. Trying to build some kind of case against me, I suppose. It's just so exhausting, having to look over my shoulder constantly when all I'm trying to do is make an honest living and keep my own house in order.

Doctor, are you... are you actually listening to the words coming out of my mouth? Or are you just reading off a list of questions on that clipboard? Because I swear we are going around in circles like a washing machine on the spin cycle. 

No. I do not see her. If I saw a strange woman standing in my kitchen, I would be dialing 911, not standing there scrubbing dishes! Like I just said, I will spin around when she speaks, and I'll drip soapy water all over the floor—which is just fantastic, because then I have to stop what I'm doing and wipe it up immediately before it seeps into the seams of the linoleum and ruins the adhesive—and there is absolutely no one there to look at. The kitchen is empty.

But the fact that I don't see her doesn't change the fact that even when the house is completely, utterly quiet, I hear her voice. Right near the kitchen window. She tells me to check the locks, she tells me to move his pills so the agency people can't find them... it is as clear as if she is standing right there next to the dish rack. I don't see a face, I don't see a body, I don't see a shadow. I just hear her. I really, truly do not know how I can make this any clearer for you.

doctor.question: Do you ever hear the woman's voice when you are not at home?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: Even when the house is quiet, I hear a woman's voice near the kitchen window telling me to check the locks or move his pills, clear as if she is standing right there.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking a follow-up question about the auditory hallucinations (hearing the woman's voice) to determine if they occur in other settings outside the home.

patient.answer:
Well, no, not really when I'm out and about. See, when I'm at work, I've got the vacuum running, or the radio on—Mrs. Henderson likes to keep the classical station playing softly while I dust her sitting room, she says it keeps the energy in the house calm, which I suppose is fine, though it does put me to sleep if I'm trying to scrub baseboards—so there's always noise. And I'm focused. I have a routine. I do the dry dusting first, then the damp wiping, then the floors. You have to work top to bottom, otherwise you're just knocking dust onto things you've already cleaned, which is a rookie mistake. 

So no, I don't hear her then. It's really just... it's just when I'm home. And it's exactly like I've been telling you. It happens when the house is completely quiet. My husband is resting, the TV is off, no radio, no vacuum, just silence. And then, right there near the kitchen window, I hear her. The woman's voice. It's as clear as if she's standing right there on the linoleum next to me while I'm at the sink. And she's telling me to go check the deadbolts, or to make sure his pills are moved out of sight so the agency people can't see them. It's only ever right there in my own kitchen, in the quiet. I don't know why she only speaks to me there, but that's where she is.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's perception of being followed is delusional
doctor.question: Do you think the woman's voice near the kitchen window could be related to the people you believe are following you?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I'm here because people keep acting like I'm imagining it, but I know the hospital people and some folks from the agency have been watching our house and my cleaning routes to see if I'm taking proper care of my husband.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about my belief that people are following or watching me, which connects to my delusions about the hospital and agency people watching my house and cleaning routes.

patient.answer:
Well, of course it is! I mean... it has to be, doesn't it? Why else would she specifically tell me to hide his medication from the agency people? That’s the whole reason I’m even sitting here in this chair talking to you today, because my family and... well, everybody, really... they keep acting like I’m just imagining the whole thing. They look at me with this pitying little smile, like I'm just an exhausted old woman making things up out of thin air. 

But I am not stupid, Doctor. I know what I see. I know for an absolute fact that the hospital people and some folks from the agency have been watching our house. And not just the house, they follow my cleaning routes, too. I'll be driving from Mrs. Henderson's place over to my next client in the Oakwood subdivision—which, by the way, is a complete nightmare right now because they've been doing road work on Elm for three months and the dust gets all over my freshly washed car, it's just a mess—and I will see them. I see them keeping tabs on me. 

They are doing it because they want to see if I'm taking proper care of my husband. As if I haven't been doing everything for him! I make sure he's comfortable, I cook him his low-sodium meals so his blood pressure stays down, I keep a spotless, completely sanitary home for him to rest in. I am doing everything right. But they are looking for any little excuse to say I'm not doing a good enough job, so they watch me. They watch the house. So yes, when that voice in the kitchen tells me to move his pills so the agency people can't snoop, she knows exactly what they are up to. She's warning me about them, because she knows they're out there watching, even if everyone else in my life wants to pretend I'm just imagining it.

doctor.question: Do you ever see things that aren't really there when you're hearing the woman's voice?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: Even when the house is quiet, I hear a woman's voice near the kitchen window telling me to check the locks or move his pills, clear as if she is standing right there.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I experience visual hallucinations (seeing things that aren't there), which falls under the Hallucinations symptom.

patient.answer:
Doctor, I... I feel like I'm talking to a brick wall here. I really do. Did you not hear what I just said a few minutes ago? I swear, I am trying my absolute hardest to be cooperative and answer all these questions, but you keep asking me the same things over and over, just slightly reworded. 

No, I do not see things that aren't there! I told you, I don't see a face, I don't see a shadow, I don't see a body. When I am standing at that kitchen sink—and I use a very specific sponge for the dishes, mind you, not the one I use for wiping down the counters, because cross-contamination is how people get sick, especially with my husband's immune system being what it is—I am just looking at the dishes, or out the window at the yard. The yard needs mowing, actually, the grass is getting entirely too high, but I just haven't had the time between work and taking care of him. 

But no, I don't see anything out of the ordinary. It is strictly the voice. Even when the house is completely, pin-drop quiet, I hear her voice right near the kitchen window. She tells me to check the locks, or she tells me to move his pills so the agency people can't find them. It is as clear as if she is standing right there on the linoleum next to me. But I don't *see* her. I don't see anything at all that isn't supposed to be there. Just the voice. I don't know how many different ways I can explain this to you, Doctor. I really don't.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's belief in being followed is delusional
doctor.question: Do you think it's possible that the people you believe are following you are just in the same places as you by coincidence?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I'm here because people keep acting like I'm imagining it, but I know the hospital people and some folks from the agency have been watching our house and my cleaning routes to see if I'm taking proper care of my husband.
target_item.reason: The doctor is challenging my belief about being followed by the hospital and agency people, asking if it could be a coincidence. This directly relates to my fixed beliefs (delusions) about them watching me.

patient.answer:
Coincidence? Doctor, please. Coincidence is when you run into the mailman at the grocery store. Coincidence is not the same silver sedan parked three houses down when I pull out of my driveway, and then that very same sedan turning onto Elm Street right behind me when I'm on my way to Mrs. Henderson's. You know, I actually memorized the first three letters of the license plate—J-K-L—because I thought, well, maybe I am just tired. Maybe my mind is playing tricks on me because I've been up since 4:30 AM making sure my husband's breakfast is prepared exactly the way he needs it. He has to have his oatmeal made with water, not milk, and a very specific ratio of cinnamon, otherwise his stomach gets upset, and I simply cannot have him getting sick on top of everything else. 

But no, it's not a coincidence. I am sitting here in this office today specifically because everyone—my family, the neighbors, everyone—keeps acting like I am just imagining this whole thing. They think I'm just a paranoid old woman who spends too much time cleaning. But I know what I see. I know for a fact that the hospital people and the folks from the agency have been watching our house. And they watch my cleaning routes, too! I see them at the Oakwood subdivision, I see them near the grocery store when I stop to get his low-sodium broth. 

They are doing it because they want to catch me slipping up. They want to see if I'm taking proper care of my husband, and they are just waiting for me to make one little mistake so they can step in. As if I haven't dedicated every waking moment to keeping that house perfectly sanitized and keeping him comfortable! So no, Doctor, it is absolutely not a coincidence. They are out there, they are watching, and I am not crazy for seeing them, no matter what anyone else tries to tell you.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's persistent delusions of being followed and monitored by hospital people and agency folks, despite lack of evidence and reassurance from others, meet the criteria for Delusional Disorder. The presence of a voice heard near the kitchen window, which is not a typical auditory hallucination but rather a specific, instructive voice, further supports this diagnosis.
